facts: The China National Space Administration (CNSA) was founded on 22 April 1993.
China's Tiangong space station has been continuously crewed since June 2022.
Tiangong consists of three pressurised modules — Tianhe (core), Wentian and Mengtian — each ~22 tonnes.
Yang Liwei was the first Chinese national in orbit, aboard Shenzhou-5 in October 2003.
The BeiDou-3 constellation reached full global operational status on 23 June 2020.
The Long March 5 is China's most powerful operational rocket, capable of ~25 tonnes to low Earth orbit.
Chang'e-3 soft-landed on the Moon in December 2013 — the first lunar soft landing by any nation since 1976.
Chang'e-4 became the first spacecraft ever to land on the far side of the Moon (3 January 2019).
Chang'e-5 returned 1.731 kg of lunar samples to Earth on 16 December 2020 — the first sample return since 1976.
Tianwen-1's Zhurong rover landed on Mars on 15 May 2021 — China's first successful Mars surface mission.
Tiangong orbits Earth roughly every 92 minutes at ~400 km altitude.
Tianzhou cargo freighters resupply Tiangong autonomously, similar to the ISS Progress vehicles.
China is the third country to independently send humans to space, after the Soviet Union and the United States.
Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan is China's lowest-latitude (~19° N) pad, giving heavy rockets an Earth-spin boost.
BeiDou uses 24 satellites in MEO plus 3 in GEO and 3 in IGSO for global coverage.
Long March 8 first flew in December 2020 and is part of China's reusable-rocket research programme.
Tiangong-1 (2011-2018) and Tiangong-2 (2016-2019) preceded the current modular space station.
FAST — the Five-hundred-metre Aperture Spherical Telescope in Guizhou — is the world's largest single-dish radio telescope.
China launched its first satellite, Dongfanghong-1, on 24 April 1970 — the fifth nation to do so.
The Yaogan series exceeds 80 satellites and is widely believed to support naval surveillance, particularly tracking surface ships.
